name: pXart
workload: Bulk generation of 16 GiB of 32-bit random numbers through a 16 KiB cache buffer, plus a 10^8-sample Monte Carlo pi benchmark, comparing std::mt19937, Boost mt19937 and pXart scalar/SSE4.1/AVX2 MT19937 and Xoroshiro128+.
claimed_speedup: Thesis Table 9.1 (i7-7700K, 4.51 GHz): 16 GiB generation takes 9.29 s with STL MT19937, 5.79 s Boost MT19937, 7.61 s pXart scalar MT19937, 2.11 s pXart SSE MT19937 and 1.15 s pXart AVX MT19937 (AVX about 8.1x faster than STL, derived from page data). Monte Carlo pi (Table 9.2): 0.53 s STL MT19937 (uniform) vs 0.07 s pXart AVX MT19937. Thesis text: scalar pXart beat the STL version but not Boost's; SSE/AVX versions are 'more than three times' / 'more than six times' faster than pXart scalar.
hardware: Intel Core i7-7700K (Kaby Lake, 4.51 GHz measured); second machine Intel Core i5-8250U laptop
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; build2 package (cppget.org badge in README)
tradeoffs: Needs an Intel CPU with SSE4.1/AVX2 for the vectorized engines. The SIMD engines interleave independent streams, so output differs from std::mt19937 and state is larger; own API (pxart::uniform, pxart::simd256::mt19937), not a drop-in std engine.
caveats: Numbers come from a 2019 master's thesis stored in the repo (not peer reviewed); the benchmark code is in the repo's benchmarks package but results appear only in the thesis PDF, not in the README. GCC 9.2 / libstdc++ only; Kaby Lake hardware; last commit 2021-01-18.
found_via: WebSearch 'header-only C++ PRNG library faster than std::mt19937 AVX2 SIMD vectorized random numbers batch generation GitHub'; README badge shows it is a build2 package on cppget.org

name: RANLUX++ (sibidanov/ranluxpp)
workload: Generation of single-precision floats from the RANLUX family: an LCG formulation of RANLUX (modulus 2^576 - 2^240 + 1, 576x576-bit modular multiplication in x86-64 assembly) versus GCC's std::ranlux and a SIMD-optimized conventional RANLUX.
claimed_speedup: README: 'generation speed achieved (20 clock/float) is order of magnitude faster than the usual approach, for example, GCC C++ RANLUX implementation where 198 clock/float is measured at Haswell CPU'; the optimized conventional RANLUX reaches 40 clock/float, and the SSE2 and AVX2 versions are 'approximately 4 and 8 times faster' than scalar.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -O3 -Iinc -mavx2, ASMSKIP enabled (from the repo Makefile)
hardware: Haswell CPU (GCC RANLUX figure) and Skylake CPU (RANLUX++ figure); microarchitecture names only, no CPU model, per README
stars_or_usage: 11 stars; later adopted in ROOT as RanluxppEngine (ROOT commit 36cc2a8 'Implement RANLUX++ generator')
tradeoffs: x86-64 assembly (mulx/adcx/adox variants chosen by GCC function multiversioning), so not portable to other architectures; LGPL-3.0 (COPYING and COPYING.LESSER in repo). The win is inside the RANLUX family: RANLUX is itself far slower than mt19937/PCG/xoshiro, so this does not beat the category baselines.
caveats: First-party README numbers with only CPU microarchitecture names; the GCC figure (198 clock/float) was measured on Haswell while RANLUX++ (20 clock/float) was measured on Skylake, so the 10x claim mixes two CPUs. The accompanying paper (Computer Physics Communications 2017, arXiv 1705.03123) could not be opened in this session (arxiv.org blocked), so no peer-review upgrade to tier B. Baseline std::ranlux is not in the category baseline list. Last commit 2018-01-17.
found_via: WebSearch 'fast random number generator C++ library benchmark faster than std::mt19937 vcpkg OR conan' surfaced arXiv 1705.03123; repo opened from a follow-up search

name: cpp_prngs (QuarkBurst64, RomuDuoJr, Konadare192 engines)
baseline: std::mt19937 (also std::minstd_rand, std::default_random_engine and C rand())
workload: Quick Bench runs of raw engine next() throughput, bounded integers and bounded floats comparing the library's engines (PCG32, Xoshiro256SS, RomuDuoJr, QuarkBurst64, Konadare192, SmallFast*) against standard-library generators.
claimed_speedup: README: 'All of the included engines substantially outperform the standard-library generators in this benchmark.' Engine-throughput chart (CPU time / no-op time, lower is faster; values read off the bar chart, approximate): std::mt19937 about 13,000; PCG32 about 5,000; Xoshiro256SS about 4,000; QuarkBurst64 and RomuDuoJr about 2,500 (roughly 5x faster than std::mt19937, derived from chart).
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 with constexpr engines; 4-32 bytes of state; deterministic across platforms; engines are ports of known algorithms (Bob Jenkins SmallFast, Romu, Pelle Evensen's konadare192px++, Eightomic quarkburst), wrapped in a game-oriented Random<E> API; the 8/16-bit engines target microcontrollers.
caveats: Results are bar-chart PNGs from Quick Bench (README commits benchmarks/results/*.png), with no numeric table and no compiler, flags or CPU stated in the repo; Quick Bench ratios are against a no-op, not absolute times. The fastest engine, QuarkBurst64, is a very new generator with limited external statistical review. The baseline is std::mt19937 directly, but the stronger baselines (PCG, xoshiro) are the same algorithms the library wraps.
found_via: WebSearch 'random number generator C++ library vcpkg OR conan benchmark ns/number std::mt19937 std::uniform_int_distribution faster bounded random Lemire library'

name: EigenRand
baseline: C++ <random> distributions (std::normal_distribution, std::uniform_real_distribution, std::uniform_int_distribution, etc.) and Eigen::DenseBase::Random
workload: Generation of whole Eigen matrices of random numbers from many univariate distributions with SSE2/AVX2/AVX512/NEON vectorized generators and Vmt19937_64 versus the equivalent non-vectorized std or Eigen calls.
claimed_speedup: README: '5~10 times faster than non-vectorized functions' and 'You can get 5~10 times speed by just replacing old Eigen's Random or unvectorizable c++11 random number generators with EigenRand'. Ubuntu/gcc 7.5/AVX2 chart (values read off the bar chart, approximate): normal(0,1) about 8x, uniformReal about 22x, uniformInt(0..63) about 10x, discrete about 32x, binomial(20,0.5) about 24x, but only about 1.6-1.7x for chiSquared, gamma(10.5,1) and uniformInt(0..100k).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 7.5.0 on Ubuntu 18.04; MSVC 19.29.30147 on Windows 2019; clang 13.1.6 on macOS 12.2.1; Eigen 3.4.0; CMake Release flags -O3 (gcc/clang) and -O2 -Oi -Gy (MSVC)
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C (AVX2, Ubuntu); Intel Xeon Platinum 8171M (AVX2, Windows); Apple M1 Pro (NEON, macOS)
tradeoffs: Requires Eigen (3.3.4 to 5.0.x). The speed-up is for bulk matrix generation and vectorization over parameters; results are not bit-identical to std distributions (vectorized math with accuracy checked by Earth Mover's Distance), and P8_mt19937_64 exists for architecture-independent streams.
caveats: Speed-ups are shown as chart images (exact values in the GitHub Actions run, not opened); the standard-library stdlib per platform is inferred from the compiler (libstdc++ / MSVC STL / libc++), and the random engine used under the std reference is not stated in the README. Several distributions are only 1.6-3x and the README notes some cases are slower than the reference (orange cells on other charts). Baselines are std distributions, not std::mt19937/PCG/xoshiro engines.
found_via: WebSearch 'faster than std::normal_distribution fast Gaussian random number generator C++ ziggurat AVX benchmark GitHub'

name: normaldist-benchmark (Ziggurat and AVX/SSE2 Box-Muller)
workload: Filling an array of 1,000,000 standard-normal samples (best of 10 trials) in float and double with Box-Muller, Marsaglia polar, Ziggurat, inverse CDF, CLT, and SSE2/AVX Box-Muller variants.
claimed_speedup: Double precision: cpp11random 32.245 ns/sample vs ziggurat 7.086 ns (page lists 4.55x). Single precision: cpp11random 18.642 ns vs ziggurat 6.731 ns and boxmuller_avx 2.253 ns (about 2.8x and 8.3x, derived from page data); boxmuller_sse2 3.752 ns.
compiler_and_flags: clang 6.1 on macOS 64-bit; premake4 release build (Optimize; gmake adds -mavx -std=c++11)
tradeoffs: Benchmark harness with standalone implementations rather than a packaged library: Ziggurat is Jochen Voss's implementation, Box-Muller SSE2/AVX use sse_mathfun/avx_mathfun approximations and need aligned buffers and n divisible by 2/8; the CLT variants fail the repo's own kurtosis check.
caveats: Every implementation except the baseline uses a simple linear congruential generator for uniforms while the baseline uses std::minstd_rand, so part of the gap is the uniform source and not the normal transform; the page's 'Speedup' column is relative to the slowest row, so the ratios against std were derived here. 2015 hardware and old clang; macOS libc++ presumably. The winners are techniques/code in the benchmark repo, not separate repos.
found_via: WebSearch 'faster than std::normal_distribution fast Gaussian random number generator C++ ziggurat AVX benchmark GitHub'

name: FastShuffleExperiments (nearly divisionless bounded random integers)
baseline: std::shuffle (same underlying PRNG), plus OpenBSD-style and Java-style bounded-integer generation
workload: Random shuffles of arrays of 5 to 10^9 elements, ns per element, with 32-bit and 64-bit random words, comparing Lemire's nearly divisionless bounded-integer method against OpenBSD-like, Java-like, floating-point and std::shuffle approaches.
claimed_speedup: README sample output (arrays of 1000 elements, ns per element): nearly divisionless 1.88 (32-bit) and 1.86 (64-bit) vs std::shuffle 18.66 and 15.28, vs OpenBSD-like 5.40 and 14.36, vs Java-like 3.08 and 7.96 (about 10x and 8x faster than std::shuffle, derived from page data); the README notes 'the exact numbers will vary'.
stars_or_usage: 41 stars; technique adopted by libstdc++ std::uniform_int_distribution, Abseil, Swift, Go, Julia, Zig, NumPy per README
tradeoffs: Needs 128-bit multiplication (__uint128_t) for 64-bit words; the buffered/precomputed variants trade memory for speed; unbiased, nearly divisionless rejection method.
caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (D. Lemire, 'Fast Random Integer Generation in an Interval', ACM TOMACS 29(1), 2019) with an RCR artifact, but the paper itself could not be opened (arxiv.org blocked); the CPU model is not stated in the README and the sample numbers are illustrative. libstdc++ has since adopted the same technique, so std::shuffle in current GCC is much closer to this result than the README sample suggests. Related repo lemire/cpp_batched_random is already catalogued.
found_via: WebSearch 'random number generator C++ library vcpkg OR conan benchmark ns/number std::mt19937 ... Lemire library' surfaced lemire/simple_cpp_shuffle_benchmark, which points to this repo

name: simdrng
baseline: std::mt19937_64 and std::uniform_real_distribution; also scalar xoshiro256++
workload: Google Benchmark runs (CI, GitHub-hosted runner) of per-call u64, per-call double and buffer fill for Xoshiro256++, ChaCha and Philox, scalar versus xsimd-dispatched SIMD, against std::mt19937_64.
claimed_speedup: gcc-15 results JSON: next() u64 std::mt19937_64 1.60 ns vs scalar xoshiro 0.94 ns; double sample std::mt19937_64 with std::uniform_real_distribution 8.01 ns vs xoshiro uniform() 1.32 ns (about 6.1x, derived); buffer fill xoshiro SIMD 2.49e9 items/s vs scalar 1.07e9 items/s (about 2.3x, derived) and vs std::mt19937_64 per-call 0.625e9/s (about 4.0x, derived). Philox4x32 SIMD fill 5.14e8/s vs scalar 1.49e8/s.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 15, CMake Release, CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS=-march=x86-64-v3 (bench preset in CMakePresets.json); also clang-19/20 and gcc-14 result sets on the same branch
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (GitHub-hosted runner, 4 vCPUs, 2.445 GHz; cpu_model.txt in results)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20 with xsimd runtime dispatch and numpy.random.Generator-compatible Python bindings (nanobind); the SIMD engines are faster only in bulk fills (single-call SIMD xoshiro is 2.81 ns vs 0.94 ns scalar) and produce lane-interleaved streams.
caveats: Run on a shared GitHub CI runner, so absolute numbers are noisy; the README says the full matrix is in a chart and the docs page (not reachable here). The license is BSD-3-Clause with an extra attribution clause (SPDX BSD-3-Clause-Attribution), which is permissive in practice but not OSI-listed as far as known, so usability is set to reference per the rubric; reclassify if the orchestrator treats it as permissive. Baseline stdlib is inferred (gcc on Linux).

name: vphilox
baseline: std::mt19937 (also compared with xoshiro256++ and PCG64)
workload: Cycles per byte of bulk random-byte generation (generate_n) and per-call operator() for a counter-based Philox4x32-10 engine with scalar/AVX2/AVX-512/NEON backends versus std::mt19937, xoshiro256++, PCG64 and unspecialised Philox on five machines.
claimed_speedup: docs/benchmarks/README.md cost per byte relative to std::mt19937 (lower is faster), vphilox generate_n: Pi 5 0.75x, Sapphire Rapids 0.38x, Skylake-SP 0.22x, Cascade Lake 4v 0.24x, Cascade Lake 32v 0.33x (README: '1.3x to 4.6x the throughput of std::mt19937'). For comparison xoshiro256++ is 0.17-0.30x and PCG64 0.32-0.83x; vphilox operator() is 0.51-1.15x.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0 (Ubuntu 24.04, x86) and GCC 12.2.0 (Debian 12, Pi 5); CMake Release 'bench' preset; run via scripts/benchmarks/run_matrix.sh with pinned CPU (taskset), 9 repetitions
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8481C (Sapphire Rapids), Intel Xeon @ 2.0 GHz Skylake-SP, Intel Xeon @ 2.8 GHz Cascade Lake (4 vCPU slice and whole 2-socket host), Raspberry Pi 5 (Cortex-A76)
tradeoffs: Counter-based (seekable in constant time, bit-identical across machines, thread-count independent output) with C++20 header-only SIMD backends chosen at runtime; the bulk generate_n path is needed for the speed (operator() goes through a refill buffer).
caveats: Beats std::mt19937 but not the stronger baselines: xoshiro256++ is faster on four of five CPUs (vphilox wins only on Skylake-SP, 0.4210 vs 0.4703 cycles per byte), and the README says so; PCG64 is slower than vphilox bulk on all five. Author-run benchmarks, mostly cloud vCPUs (shared hosts), reference-cycle counters that only compare within a machine; the project is days old and says it has not been tagged yet.

name: PhiloxSIMD (syed-ahmed/benchmark-rngs)
workload: Time to produce 134,217,728 random 32-bit values on 1 to 1024 threads, comparing AVX2 Philox (philox_simd), scalar Philox, xoshiro256**, PCG64, PyTorch at::mt19937 and std::mt19937.
claimed_speedup: results/README.md, 1 thread, best average seconds for 134217728 randoms: philox_simd (global) 0.176, philox_simd (thread local) 0.188, philox scalar 0.439, at::mt19937 0.393, xoshiro256** 0.651, PCG64 0.659, std::mt19937 1.609 (philox_simd about 9.1x faster than std::mt19937 and 3.7x faster than xoshiro256** and PCG64, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GNU 7.4.0; CMake with -std=c++11 -Wall -pthread -march=native, built with -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release per README
hardware: 16 x Intel Xeon E5-1660 v4 @ 3.20GHz (1 socket), Ubuntu 18.04, turbo boost off, performance governor
stars_or_usage: 4 stars; PhiloxSIMD.h uses PyTorch ATen-style (at::) code
tradeoffs: AVX2-only Philox4x32 implementation (philox_simd_engine::next32 returns eight lanes of four words) that is a benchmark harness header, not a packaged library; counter-based so streams are splittable and thread-friendly.
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo (PhiloxSIMD.h derives from PyTorch at:: code, which is BSD-style upstream), so usability is reference. The loops are not identical across engines (std::mt19937 loop overwrites z each call, 32-bit step versus 64-bit xoshiro/PCG steps versus 8x32-bit philox_simd lanes), whole-loop timings include a mutex taken once per thread, and absolute ns per number look slow for xoshiro and mt19937 (about 9.7 ns and 12 ns), so treat ratios with care. 2019 hardware and GCC 7.4.

name: MELG-64 (MELG19937-64)
workload: CPU time to generate 10^9 64-bit unsigned integers with MELG19937-64, MT19937-64, MT19937-64 (ID3), SFMT19937-64 without SIMD and SFMT19937-64 with SIMD.
claimed_speedup: README table: MELG19937-64 4.2123 s (Intel) / 6.2920 s (AMD) vs MT19937-64 5.1002 s / 6.6490 s (about 1.21x and 1.06x faster, derived from page data); SFMT19937-64 with SIMD is faster at 1.8457 s / 2.8806 s. The paper's main claim is maximal equidistribution (Delta 0 vs 7820 for MT19937-64) at MT-like speed.
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 (3.40GHz) and AMD Phenom II X6 1045T (2.70 GHz)
tradeoffs: Plain C, 312-word state like MT19937-64; jump-ahead for disjoint streams; recommends using most significant bits; no SIMD path.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (Harase and Kimoto, ACM TOMS 2018) but the timing harness is not in the repo (the C file's main does not time) and the baseline is the reference MT19937-64 C code, not std::mt19937_64; the speedup over MT is modest (6-21%) and SFMT with SIMD beats MELG. Licensing is inconsistent: LICENSE.md is MIT (2021) while the source file header says free for personal, academic or non-commercial use and to contact the author for commercial use, hence usability mixed. Last commit 2023-03-18.

name: SFMT (SIMD-oriented Fast Mersenne Twister)
workload: CPU time to generate 10^9 64-bit unsigned integers from SFMT19937-64 with and without SIMD versus MT19937-64, as measured in the MELG-64 README.
claimed_speedup: MELG-64 README table: SFMT19937-64 with SIMD 1.8457 s (Intel i7-3770) and 2.8806 s (AMD Phenom II X6) vs MT19937-64 5.1002 s and 6.6490 s (about 2.8x and 2.3x faster, derived from page data); without SIMD 4.2654 s and 5.6123 s (about 1.2x faster on both).
compiler_and_flags: Linux gcc -O3 (as stated in the MELG-64 README)
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 (3.40GHz) and AMD Phenom II X6 1045T (2.70 GHz)
tradeoffs: 128-bit SIMD-oriented generator tuned for 32-bit output; larger equidistribution gap than MT19937-64 (Delta 14095 vs 7820 per the MELG-64 table); README warns big-endian and AltiVec paths are not tested at all; the 32-bit output speed claims (the project's own) were not verifiable here.
caveats: The SFMT project page and paper (Saito and Matsumoto, MCQMC 2006) sit on hiroshima-u.ac.jp, which was blocked in this session, so the numbers are third-party ones from the MELG-64 authors' README table (the same authors' paper, Harase and Kimoto, ACM TOMS 2018, is peer reviewed, but it was not opened here). Baseline is the MT19937-64 reference C code, not std::mt19937_64 itself. No SIMD-vs-std::mt19937 measurement on current hardware.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/mersenne-twister?l=c%2B%2B; benchmark data from the MELG-64 README

name: ra_prng (ra_core singleblock)
workload: Wall-clock generation of batches of up to 255 words (K=255) and single-word reinitialise-per-call use (K=1), plus long streams, comparing the array-permutation generator ra_core_singleblock/orbit against xoshiro256** and Philox4x32-10 with the code inlined the same way.
claimed_speedup: README table (2026-09-12): ra_core_singleblock K=255 real throughput 20018.1 MB/s vs Xoshiro256** K=255 2937.2 MB/s and Philox4x32-10 K=255 1007.9 MB/s ('~19.9x faster than Philox and ~6.8x faster than Xoshiro256**'); at K=1, 307.3 MB/s vs xoshiro 544.8 MB/s, i.e. slower.
tradeoffs: C library with a roughly 2 KB state (two 256-entry arrays permuting each other); explicitly not cryptographic; the fast mode only pays off for batches (K=255) and loses to xoshiro256** at K=1; the orbit (long-stream) mode is about 3.2x slower than xoshiro256** per the README.
caveats: Own benchmark by the author, in a regime (K=255 batches, steady-state loop cost shown as '~0.00 ns/word') chosen where the generator wins; the README documents an earlier benchmark fairness bug (reference generators were un-inlined) and a retracted earlier claim, so numbers may keep moving. Statistical testing is thin (PractRand clean to 8 GB for K=1/K=255, to 128 GB for ra_prng2; BigCrush for ra_prng2). CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 is a non-commercial share-alike license and not an OSI software license, so the code is reference only. Not a C++ library per se (C API callable from C++).
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/prng?l=c (listed as ooalahhq/ra_prng); README opened directly

name: SIMD-MT
baseline: std::mt19937 (also std::uniform_real_distribution, lrand48, drand48, POSIX random)
workload: Google Benchmark per-call latency of next() for header-only SIMD-friendly Mersenne Twister engines with 8 interleaved streams (IRNG for integers, FRNG for floats) versus a reference scalar MT, std::mt19937 and libc generators.
claimed_speedup: README (Travis CI run 2020-05-18): BM_IRNG_next 2.32 ns, BM_FRNG_next 2.31 ns, reference MT next 3.45 ns, std::mt19937 6.33 ns, std::uniform_real_distribution 6.84 ns (about 2.7x faster than std::mt19937 for integers and 3.0x faster than std::uniform_real_distribution for floats, derived from page data).
hardware: Travis CI VM, '2 X 2800.17 MHz CPU s' (no CPU model), L2 1024 KiB, L3 33792 KiB
tradeoffs: Header-only; compiler-vectorized loops over 8 interleaved MT streams, so output is not the same sequence as std::mt19937 and the state is 8x larger; alignment and stream count are template parameters.
caveats: Only one CI log in the README: compiler, flags and CPU model are not stated, and the author says the edge over the reference implementation is smaller on his laptop. Numbers are per-call latency in a microbenchmark loop. Last commit 2020-05-18.

name: Seiran128 (prng-seiran)
baseline: MT19937-64 (std::mt19937_64 algorithm), also xoshiro256** and xoroshiro128+
workload: 64-bit outputs per nanosecond measured with the xoshiro/xoroshiro speed harness for Seiran128 against xoroshiro128+, xoshiro256**, lehmer128, splitmix, mt19937_64 and PCG64.
claimed_speedup: README table (64-bit outputs per ns): Seiran128 1.20, xoroshiro128+ 1.13, xoshiro256** 0.99, mt19937_64 0.32, PCG64 0.38; README: 'About 3.7 times faster than Mersenne Twister (64-bit version)' (about 1.2x over xoshiro256**, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Minimal C LFSR-style generator with 128-bit state and 2^128-1 period, constant-time jump of 2^64 steps, no 128-bit multiply; README says its state can be recovered from three outputs (Z3), so it is for games and simulation only.
caveats: Public-domain dedication (CC0, no patent grant). Compiler flags are not stated, and the speed comparison against xoshiro256** is a small margin on one machine with GCC 7.3. The baseline is the reference mt19937-64 C code, not std::mt19937_64. The README gives PractRand to 32 TB and BigCrush results. Last commit 2021-01-30.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/prng?l=c (listed as andanteyk/prng-seiran)
